en: The Sūtra on the Merits of Faith in the Buddha, Spoken by the Buddha.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperial Envoy, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments,
Great Master of Enlightened Teaching, Subject Faxian, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Āmra Grove in the city of Aṇḍaka together with a great assembly.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, having dressed and taken his bowl at the hour of eating, entered the city of Aṇḍaka. Having gone through the city begging for alms in due order, he returned to his dwelling, put away his robe, washed his feet, spread out his seat, and ate.
Having finished his meal, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side. Joining his palms toward the Buddha, he spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!”
I now give rise to profound faith in the Buddha.

Why is this? It is because the Buddha’s supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are supreme and peerless; among all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the past, present, and future, there is not even one who can fathom the Buddha’s supernormal powers, let alone surpass them!
"How could one possibly realize unsurpassed bodhi?
The Buddha said,
"Excellent!"
Excellent, Śāriputra!
You have been able to skillfully explain this profound and vast meaning; you should uphold it and let out a lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, proclaiming it extensively for all.
Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The faith I have now conceived toward the Buddha is such that none among those of the past, future, or present can equal it.”
Furthermore, there are no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who understand the Buddha’s penetration or surpass the Buddha; how could they possibly realize unsurpassed bodhi?
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“What do you think?”

All Buddhas of the three periods of time—Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—who possess pure ethical discipline, wisdom, liberation, and the wondrous practices of supernormal powers, I fully know through my own supernormal power;
and those Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas likewise know all that I possess of pure ethical discipline, wisdom, liberation, and the wondrous practices of supernormal powers.
"Śāriputra! Do not think that only the present Śākyamuni Buddha possesses this supernormal power.
Śāriputra said:
"No, World-Honored One! I do not say:
'Only the Buddha possesses these supernormal powers.'"
"I know that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the three periods of time are entirely equal in their pure precepts, wisdom, liberation, supernatural powers, and sublime conduct."
The Buddha said: “Śāriputra, it is so, it is so!”
All Buddhas of the three periods of time—Tathāgatas, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—possess these dharmas of supernatural powers and so forth.

You should simply proclaim such profound dharmas for the sake of those sentient beings; receive and uphold them with a single mind, and within the great assembly, let out the lion’s roar and explain them extensively.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Regarding the vast, profound, and most supreme sublime Dharma proclaimed by our Buddha—even down to wholesome and unwholesome karmas and all dharmas arisen through conditions—I have understood each and every one of them as they truly are.”
Having understood one dharma, one further cultivates another; having cultivated one dharma, one further extinguishes another; having extinguished one dharma, one further realizes another.
For this reason, I now give rise to faith in the Buddha as the truly and perfectly awakened one (samyak-saṃbuddha).
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Go now and ask others:

'In past ages, was there any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who was able to truly understand supernormal powers and other qualities surpassing those of the Buddha, even unto the attainment of Buddhahood and bodhi?'"
"You should go and ask him; what will he answer?
Furthermore, Śāriputra, you should again go there and ask others:"
"In future ages, might there be śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas equal to the Buddha, even unto the attainment of Buddhahood and bodhi?
You should go and ask him; what will he answer?
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, you may go there and ask others again:
'In the present world, are there any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who are equal to the Buddha, even unto the attainment of Buddhahood and bodhi?'"
"Furthermore, Śāriputra! Again, go there and ask others:
'Throughout all the past, future, and present worlds, to whom do the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas take refuge?'"
“You should go and ask him; what will he answer?
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
This interpretation is not correct.
I have heard from the Buddha, and I remember and uphold it: two Buddhas do not appear simultaneously in the world.
Only the World-Honored Buddha is the truly and perfectly awakened one, the one who possesses right and universal knowledge, and is endowed with the power of supreme supernormal faculties.
"World-Honored One!
I do not see any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who is able to know this supernormal power, much less one who surpasses the Buddha, even unto the attainment of Buddhahood and bodhi."
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I see that the World-Honored One possesses various most supreme dharmas. As for these most supreme dharmas, it means that when the Buddha, the World-Honored One, preaches the Dharma, he is fully able to know all the wholesome benefits thereby obtained.”

If there are śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others who dwell among mountains, forests, beneath trees, in cemeteries, or in empty huts; who enter samādhi, sever all afflictions, cultivate them to perfection, increase wholesome dharmas, and maintain right mindfulness; and if those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas sever all unwholesome dharmas and cultivate wholesome dharmas, even unto the attainment of the fruit of realization—the Buddha is able to know all such dharmas as these, and this is called the most supreme dharma of the Buddha.
There is no śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who possesses supernatural power exceeding that of the Buddha, even unto the attainment of the Bodhi of a Buddha.

"Furthermore, our Buddha, the World-Honored One, is endowed with the most supreme dharmas; that is to say, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is well able to discern the dharmas of the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) and is able to extensively proclaim them for others. There is no śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who can fully understand these twelve bases or discern them."

The twelve bases (āyatana) are as follows: the eye base and the form base; the ear base and the sound base; the nose base and the odor base; the tongue base and the taste base; the body base and the tangible base; and the mind base and the mental-object base.

Regarding such dharmas as these, only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is able to fully comprehend them; this is precisely what is called the Buddha’s most supreme dharma. There are no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who surpass the Buddha, even up until the attainment of Buddhahood and bodhi.

"Furthermore, our Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses a most supreme dharma: namely, that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is well able to thoroughly understand the principles of the dharma regarding *pudgala*, and to teach them to others; whereas no śramaṇas, brahmins, or others know such a dharma, nor can they teach it to others."

Regarding the dharmas of the *pudgala*, there are seven types: namely, the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), the follower by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), the one resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), the one attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), the bodily witness (*kāyasākṣin*), the one liberated through wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*), and the one doubly liberated (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).
These seven supreme qualities of the seven types of individuals can be fully known only by the Buddha, the World-Honored One; this is precisely what is called the most excellent dharma of the Buddha.

"Furthermore, our Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses the most supreme dharma: namely, that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, utters words of truth without falsehood, and is free from frivolous speech as well as divisive speech."

The words that issue forth are a true great benefit and the most supreme Dharma; they possess causes and conditions and are able, amidst the great assembly, to produce subtle and wondrous sounds to expound profound meanings. Such is this unsurpassed and true Dharma, which only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can fully comprehend; this is precisely what is called the Buddha’s most supreme Dharma.

"Furthermore, our Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses a most supreme dharma: namely, that through *samāpatti*, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, contemplates his own impure and loathsome body with outflows (*sāsrava*). That is to say, from the upper to the lower parts of the body—hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, tendons, and bones—his body is filled with such various impure things."
The Buddha knows them all: that these are not ultimate and are to be loathed and abandoned; this is called the first *samāpatti*.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!"

If there are śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others who, regarding all the skin, flesh, bones, marrow, and various foul, impure, and tainted things belonging to their own bodies above and below, are able to contemplate them as they truly are with wisdom, this is the second samāpatti.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
If there is a śramaṇa who, with wisdom, contemplates the body as subject to outflows (āsrava), exhausting this single lifetime yet not reaching the ultimate end—
if one can contemplate in such a manner, this is the third samāpatti."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
If there is a śramaṇa who, by means of wisdom, contemplates the body with outflows, seeing that it is not perfected in this present life, nor even in future lives.
If one can contemplate in this manner, this constitutes the fourth *samāpatti*.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

If there is a śramaṇa who, by means of wisdom, observes the body subject to outflows (*sāsrava*) as before—seeing that it is not ultimate in this life or future lives, and is not ultimate even in successive future lives, being impure and loathsome."
If one can contemplate in this manner, this is the fifth *samāpatti*.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

Such things as these—impure, defiled, and non-ultimate phenomena—are all seen by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, with his pure divine eye that surpasses the fleshly eye. He perceives the birth and death, the beautiful and the ugly, the good and evil destinies, and even rebirth in the celestial realms of all sentient beings, knowing them all as they truly are. This is precisely what is called the most supreme dharma of the Buddha."

"Furthermore, our Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses the most supreme and excellent Dharma; that is to say, when the World-Honored One teaches the Dharma, if there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who turn toward it to listen and receive it, seeking tranquility, they all rely upon the seven factors of enlightenment."

The seven factors of enlightenment are: the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment of energy, the factor of enlightenment of joy, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, the factor of enlightenment of equanimity, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, and the factor of enlightenment of concentration.
These seven dharmas are fully understood only by the Buddha, the World-Honored One; they are thus called the most supreme dharmas of the Buddha.
Furthermore, our Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses a most supreme dharma, namely, his skillful discernment of the four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*).

The four right efforts are: to abandon evil that has already been committed, to prevent the arising of evil not yet committed, to increase the good that has already been cultivated, and to bring about the production of good not yet cultivated.
Such teachings as these are extensively proclaimed among gods and humans to bring about their benefit; this is precisely what is called the Buddha’s most supreme Dharma.

"Furthermore, our Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses a most supreme dharma: namely, that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is able to manifest great supernormal powers through right knowledge."

As for these supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they consist of manifesting many from one and condensing many into one; or manifesting emptiness and non-existence; or manifesting city walls, mountains, and rocks following one’s body; or manifesting the reaching out of a hand from the earth to touch the void up to the Brahma realm; or manifesting walking upon water as if on land; or manifesting sitting cross-legged in mid-air; or manifesting the manner of movement, like the sun and moon traveling through the sky. If there are śramaṇas, brahmins, or others who, seeing such supernormal powers, give rise to disbelief, I declare them all to be deluded ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*). They are not noble ones (*ārya*); they do not possess supernormal powers; they do not seek perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), nor do they delight in seeking the tranquility of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, this supernormal power is precisely what is called the Buddha’s most supreme dharma.
"Moreover, World-Honored One!

Regarding the worldly desires for pleasing forms, beautiful forms, and so forth—whenever there are those who seek them—the Tathāgata acts according to the faculties of those sentient beings; this is precisely what is called the Tathāgata’s supernormal power."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

Regarding all forms in the world—whether pleasing or unpleasing, wholesome or unwholesome—one remains detached from both, dwelling in equanimity; and one possesses the clear knowledge of past lives. This is precisely what is called the supernormal power of the Tathāgata."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
To perceive form within form is precisely what is called the supernatural power (ṛddhi) of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
“Having no perception of internal form, one sees external forms; this is called the supernatural power (ṛddhi) of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, World-Honored One, the body is well-liberated and one realizes the mastery of movement and stillness; this is called the supernatural power of the Tathāgata.”
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
The definitive realization of the sphere of infinite space is what is called the supernatural power of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
The definitive realization of the sphere of infinite consciousness is what is called the supernatural power of the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
the definitive realization of the sphere of nothingness is what is called the supernatural power of the Tathāgata."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
The definitive realization of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is precisely what is called the supernatural power (abhijñā) of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
To fully understand feeling and perception, and for feeling and perception to be extinguished—this is what is called the supernatural power (ṛddhi) of the Tathāgata.
Such supreme spheres of supernatural power as these can be fully understood only by the Buddha, the World-Honored One; this is what is called the Buddha’s power of supernatural penetration.

"Furthermore, our Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses a most supreme dharma: namely, regarding all matters such as the causes, conditions, karmic retributions, and recollections of past lives—whether one or many—as well as the lifespan of śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others, I am unable to know them even after millions of years."
O World-Honored Buddha!

You alone know the various places where those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas dwelt throughout past times—whether in the realm of form, the formless realm, the sphere of perception, the sphere of non-perception, or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—and you fully comprehend all their diverse activities, causes, conditions, fruits, and retributions; this is precisely what is called the most supreme dharma of the Buddha.
"Furthermore, our Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses the most supreme Dharma: namely, when the World-Honored One preaches the Dharma, he always speaks in accordance with reality.

There may be certain śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others who, due to their ignorance, give rise to thoughts of 'self' and 'other,' and harbor doubts, claiming that the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma consists solely of conventional signs and verbal expressions; that the Dharma he teaches is spoken identically throughout the three periods of time; and that whether concerning what is near or far, as well as the phenomena of mind and mental factors, he speaks in this same manner—asserting that all such teachings of his are not in accordance with reality."
The Buddha is fully able to know those who harbor such doubts; this is called the most supreme teaching of the Buddha.
Furthermore, when our World-Honored Buddha preaches the Dharma, if there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who do not themselves give rise to doubt, but later hear someone say:
"The Dharma taught by the Buddha is not in accordance with reality."

Having heard these words, he again gave rise to doubt, thinking: "The World-Honored One speaks in terms of phenomenal characteristics; even those who give rise to such slander, the Buddha is able to know—this is precisely what is called the most supreme teaching of the Buddha."

"Furthermore, when our Buddha, the World-Honored One, teaches the Dharma, there may be śramaṇas, brahmins, and others who originally harbor no doubts and do not regard the World-Honored One’s discourse on phenomena as mere conventional description. Yet later, hearing the words of others, they follow them and give rise to doubt; they then speak of it to others, causing them also to fall into uncertainty. Because of this uncertainty, they conceive thoughts of 'self' and 'other,' saying: 'These matters are as before—none are true; these are merely the various and divergent minds of sentient beings.'"
The Buddha fully understands all such matters; this is precisely what is called the Buddha’s most supreme dharma.
Furthermore, when our Buddha, the World-Honored One, sees a śramaṇa in samādhi who is without doubt and without speech, the Buddha is able to fully know that person’s conduct and vows.

Furthermore, if the Buddha perceives that a śramaṇa has emerged from meditative concentration, he knows the reasons for his emergence—whether it be due to some specific matter or because of lingering doubts—and the Buddha resolves all such doubts; this is called the most supreme dharma of the Buddha.
"Furthermore, our Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses a most supreme dharma: namely, that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is well able to fully comprehend all dharmas that are not ultimate.

Suppose there were a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa dwelling in the mountains, abiding in a state of meditative equipoise, who by means of his own supernormal power knew the events of twenty eons of increase and decrease. He would think:
'Regarding all the events of the eons of increase and decrease within the past, I am able to know them all. "
"World-Honored One!
Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are unable to know matters of increase and decrease regarding the future and the present.
Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, fully knows such matters of increase and decrease throughout the three periods of time; this is called knowing the first dharma that is not ultimate."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

If there are śramaṇas, brahmins, or others who dwell in deep mountains and abide in a state of meditative equipoise, they may, by means of their own supernormal powers, know the events of forty eons of increase and decrease."
He thinks to himself:
"In future ages, all that shall increase or decrease, I have already fully known.
World-Honored One!
Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas do not know the matters of the kalpas of increase and decrease in the past and present;
only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, fully knows the three periods of time—this is called thoroughly understanding the second dharma that is not ultimate.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

If there are śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others who dwell in deep mountains, abiding in a state of meditative equipoise, they may, by means of their own supernormal powers, know the events of eighty eons of increase and decrease."
He thought to himself:
"I am able to know all matters concerning the increase and decrease of the past and the future.
World-Honored One!
Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas can only know the limits of this present life, yet they do not understand them.
Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, understands the limits of the three periods of time in their entirety; this is precisely what is called "understanding the third dharma that is not ultimate."

In this way, with the pure divine eye that surpasses the fleshly eye, the World-Honored One perceives the phenomena of the birth and death of sentient beings, even unto their rebirth in the heavenly realms; this is called the most supreme dharma of the Buddha.

"Furthermore, our Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses a most supreme dharma: namely, that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, through the dharma of discipline, thoroughly understands the dharmas in which various *pudgalas* delight, and accordingly teaches them."

Once this person has understood this, they practice accordingly, severing the three afflictions and before long realizing the fruit of *srotāpanna*. They go against the current of birth and death, going seven times to the heavens and returning seven times to the human realm, reaching the end of suffering; thus, the World-Honored One knows all of this completely.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!

You know the dispositions of those individuals and how they practice according to the Dharma; you know that they will sever the three afflictions and eliminate greed, hatred, and delusion, and before long realize the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, returning once more to the human realm to reach the end of suffering—all this, World-Honored One, you fully understand.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!

You well know the dispositions of individuals and their dharmas; practicing according to principle, they sever the five afflictions and secondary afflictions and will before long realize the fruit of Anāgāmin—all this, World-Honored One, you fully understand.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!

You well know individuals who practice according to the principle; before long, their outflows are exhausted, and they realize the Dharma of liberation, [attaining] the realization that "birth has been exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence."
"The Tathāgata fully understands each and every such phenomenon; this is precisely what is called the Buddha’s most supreme dharma.

Furthermore, our Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses a most supreme dharma, namely that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is well able to understand the four kinds of embryonic gestation: first, those who are unaware of entering the womb, and likewise unaware of staying therein or emerging from it;
second, those who are aware of entering the womb, but are unaware of staying therein or emerging from it;"
Third, there are those who are aware of entering and abiding in the womb, but not of emerging from it;
fourth, there are those who are fully aware of entering, abiding, and emerging.
These four types differ in their awareness; only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, understands each of them individually, and this is precisely what is called the most supreme dharma of the Buddha.

"Furthermore, our Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses a most supreme dharma: namely, that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is perfectly able to discern all *pudgalas*, such that they realize the fruits of sainthood according to the obstacles they have severed."
The Buddha fully understands all such dharmas; this is precisely what is called the Buddha’s most supreme dharma.

Furthermore, our Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses a most supreme dharma: namely, that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, thoroughly knows those who have already perfected the faculty of faith, whose conduct is pure, who are endowed with wisdom, who are truthful and without falsehood, who are without self and without indolence, who are free from all delusions, who are without distraction, and who are without greed; who do not lead or show sentient beings by way of false paths, but always practice right mindfulness.
"Such dharmas as these can be fully understood only by the Buddha, the World-Honored One; this is precisely what is called the Buddha’s most supreme dharma.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
All foolish worldlings in this world crave various sensual pleasures; they exhaust their own bodies in toil, seeking only that which is meaningless and without benefit.

The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are not like this: they delight solely in benefiting others and do not seek their own pleasure. Having thoroughly understood the nature of the mind, they perceive the tranquility of all phenomena, abide in the state of peace and bliss, and—free from desire and free from suffering—attain the four dhyānas.
Therefore, World-Honored One, if there are sons of good family with superior faculties who see thus, hear thus, perceive thus, and know thus, they are called those of truly superior faculties.
At that time, there was a venerable one in the assembly named Nāgārakṣita, who stood attending to the Buddha’s side, holding a precious fly-whisk in his hand.
Then, the venerable Nāgārakṣita addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

I have observed that various heterodox outsiders, such as the Nirgranthas, did not first give rise to faith in the Buddha, the World-Honored One; instead, they vied with one another to proclaim the superior efficacy of their own false paths.

Therefore, I now establish this stupa with its banner and proclaim it to the world, so that all may hear and know the supreme merits of the Buddha. Our Buddha, the World-Honored One, is a Great Man, most honored and most supreme; there is no one equal to him.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Nāgārjuna, saying:
"Do not speak thus; do not proclaim to others the supreme merits of the Buddha, for I do not wish to have them extolled in such a manner."
Thereupon, the Venerable Nāgārjuna praised the World-Honored One, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"This is the truly perfect, complete enlightenment.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra:

"You should skillfully propagate and proclaim this True Dharma extensively for bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas and upāsikās, as well as for all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas—even for all those of wrong views who do not believe in the Buddha, such as the Māras, non-Buddhists, and Nirgranthas—so that upon hearing this True Dharma, they may give rise to deep faith, turn toward the Buddha, develop right view, and come to understand the True Dharma."
He further addressed him, saying:
"You, Śāriputra, should propagate and proclaim it in this manner."
At that time, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Śāriputra,
"I have finished speaking," and remained silent.
Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra, having received the Buddha’s majestic power and spoken this Dharma, prostrated to the Buddha and withdrew.
At that time, the entire assembly, having heard the True Dharma, rejoiced, paid their respects, and accepted it with faith to put it into practice.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Merit of Faith in the Buddha
